Game examples

Open collection
Game example

Katana Kitsune: Prototype

Choose a kitsune fighter and face yokai in an isometric action roguelike with katana combat, stamina, pickups and successive dungeon floors. The silent prototype supports local multiplayer, with additional party systems documented in the current source.

Game example

Overexposed

Guide a rising performer through a year of career choices in a card-based fame simulation. Play cards to build craft, money and attention while three newspapers react and excessive heat turns into scandals.

Game example

Polar Icecapade

Slide across icy 3D arenas, use a three-hit melee combo to propel yourself forward, and fire projectiles that push you backward. Open gates and collect coins while confronting a rat regime in a short game-jam adventure.

Game example

Minimal Rogue

Explore a monochrome dungeon, break blocks, manage stamina and equipment, and descend through an ASCII-style roguelike with English and Japanese interfaces.

Game example

Word Rain

Move a basket to catch letters in the right order, complete shuffled words and survive red hazards. Shields, wildcards, perfect-word streaks and changing falling speed add decisions to the arcade spelling loop.

Game example

8-Second Crew · 8초 도둑단

Record an eight-second route, replay it as a clone and cooperate with earlier selves to steal a key and escape. Nine stages introduce pressure plates, patrols and projectiles.

Game example

Core Business

Drill for minerals, manage fuel and hull condition, and spend earnings at surface shops in a non-commercial mining tech demo inspired by Motherload. Three.js renders the 2.5D world while Blender scripts produce its 3D assets.

Game example

Vibe Golf

Charge and release shots across a hilly, prop-filled 3D landscape while chasing moving duck targets in a small arcade golf sandbox.

Game example

Fang the Fox · Game Boy Color

Explore floating islands, fight bosses, solve puzzles and follow a fox’s adventure as a real Game Boy Color game, playable through a browser emulator or a handheld ROM.

Game example

Three Kingdoms: Hundred Heroes

Manage gold and grain, develop cities and command officers across fifteen strongholds. Choose Wei, Shu or Wu and compete with two computer factions to unify the map.

Game example

Pelican on a Bike

Ride a helmeted pelican along a procedural coast, change lanes to catch fish, jump and unlock small achievements. The complete Three.js project includes its own character, bicycle, ocean, audio and day/night systems.

Game example

Fishslop

Pilot a bathyscaphe through a sunken reef, feed fish, collect the coins they drop and buy new residents or submarine parts. Sonar briefly reveals an otherwise invisible Veilfin.

Game example

Clock Out Unseen

Sneak out of three offices before time expires, using furniture, coffee distractions and a temporary folder disguise to avoid patrol sightlines and reach an elevator.

Game example

Nagi Home

Care for Nagi, a small crab living in a procedural home: place food, throw a ball, request furniture activities and follow a diary as daily needs change. It is a quiet life simulation with saved progress.

Game example

THUNDERFALL · Skyward Expedition

Choose one of three fighters and weave through five sectors of drifting bullets, lasers and bosses. Collect four weapon colors and pick upgrades between stages.

Game example

Fruit Ninja Dojo · One More Slice

Swipe through airborne fruit, chain slices and dodge bombs in an unofficial Fruit Ninja recreation with Classic, sixty-second Arcade and ninety-second Zen modes.

Game example

Pixel Orchard · Memory Harvest

Turn over twelve seed packets to find six matching symbol pairs. Track moves, remember mismatches and reshuffle the garden for another short round.

Game example

Butch Graves 3D

Fight through five Halloween shooter episodes with bosses, keys, secrets and scripted cutscenes, rendered by a compact raycasting engine for Java feature phones.

Game example

IsoCity

Build an isometric city with zoning, roads, rail, utilities and a simulated population. IsoCity is a complete Canvas-based browser game that its creator attributes to Cursor.

Game example

Project Plateau: Proof Before Dark

A first-person field-photography expedition inspired by The Lost World: frame prehistoric animals, manage four photographic plates, avoid threats and return to camp before daylight fades.

Game example

SURGE for Oinja

Shape an electrical build while surviving mechanical swarms across two interactive maps. Automatic attacks leave movement, dodging, upgrades and facility restoration to the player.

Game example

DEEP YELLOW

Explore procedural Backrooms in a first-person, turn-based roguelike. Moving or waiting triggers combat, while equipment combinations and sanity shape each run.

Game example

morBreaker

Clear ten brick-breaker levels with a paddle-controlled ball that accelerates on bounces, rising brick durability, and locally saved high scores.

Game example

Silent Meridian

Investigate an observatory trapped at 00:17, compare Present and Echo states, and solve thirteen connected puzzles across four chapters with a journal and optional hints.

Game example

Castle Clash Duel

Recruit warriors and archers and fight a two-player tactical battle on a tilemap. This complete Phaser prototype pairs Claude Code implementation with Pixel Frog’s Tiny Swords artwork.

Game example

Golden Hour Skatepark

Skate an original beachside park: carve transitions, ollie, flip, grind, manual, bail and recover. This complete third-person sandbox has transient trick combos and a changeable time of day, with no levels or persistent score.

Game example

Vibe Racer

A top-down time-trial racer with saved best laps, player and creator ghosts, mud surfaces, and a built-in track editor.

Game example

Journey to the West: Three Borrowings of the Banana Fan

A Chinese turn-based RPG with painted walking maps, quests, equipment, pets and command battles, adapted from the Banana Fan chapters of Journey to the West.

Game example

Clowder & Crest

Recruit cats into a medieval guild, take jobs across fifteen minigame types, develop bonds and follow a seven-chapter campaign shaped by the guild’s reputation.

Game example

Pokemon Tactics

Move Pokemon across an isometric battlefield, use elevation and aim area attacks without hitting allies. This playable tactical fan game combines a TypeScript simulation with 2D-HD sprites on Babylon.js terrain.

Game example

Rhythm Master 3D

A four-lane music game with generated synth tracks, difficulty settings, combos and a special mode, implemented as a single browser HTML file.

Game example

Spirit of Kiro

Find unusual items, combine or transform them on a workshop bench, and sell the results to an AI appraiser in an open-ended crafting game.

Game example

IsoCoaster

Game example

Astra Floor

Fight six zombie waves and a final boss in a first-person industrial arena, managing ammunition, recoil, stamina and purchases between rounds.

Game example

Mosswing

Keep a small creature airborne with one-tap flaps, pass scrolling stone gaps and chase a higher score in a compact 3D browser game.

Game example

Sprout Quest

Claude Dreaming

Walk from a pixel-art attic into playable 3D paintings: a dream garden, space flight, small planets, and community-built rooms.

Magic Carpet Wizard · A Thousand Skies

Fly a carpet over a tiny spherical world, thread scoring rings, cast three spells and face roaming enemies and bosses. Local ghost races let two players take turns.

Supermarket Simulator

The official README explicitly names several coding agents, and the skills contain practical API examples linked to engine source.

GodotPrompter: multi-agent Godot skills and reusable movement code

Agent resource

Playgama: web-game performance skill and executable probes

A reusable skill that measures a running game after warm-up and guides performance fixes using frame time, JavaScript cost, draw calls, and triangles. It includes both a headless measurement script and an in-game probe for real-device observation.

Agent resource

Playgama: asset-production skill and GLB/audio build pipeline

A coding-agent skill for choosing a coherent asset set, recording credits, and preparing it for shipping. Its executable pipeline cleans and compresses GLB models while preserving names, handles audio conversion, and can re-encode textures.

Agent resource

GameDev Agent Skills: engine router and test/code recipes

A community skill library whose router detects the project’s engine and loads task-specific guidance. Beyond a directory of links, it contains the actual skill bodies, source-backed code recipes, a skill validator, and asset-report/preview utilities.

Agent resource

Aider: an official Pong build transcript with real code edits

Aider’s own example records building Pong and then changing paddle colors, size, and ball behavior. It exposes the actual edit blocks and applied Git commits, making the incremental coding workflow inspectable rather than presenting an unexplained final screenshot.

Development paths

Open collection
Development path

Build a 2D game

A small, repeatable path from a game brief to a distributable build.

Development path

Build a 3D game

Start with one space, establish a working loop, and prepare game-ready assets.

Development path

Explore code world models

Define state and actions, connect rendering, and test what persists.

Steps & checkpoints

Open collection
Path step

Plan & scope

Define player actions, win and loss conditions, and the target platform. Keep the first version focused on one repeatable core loop.

Path step

Choose an engine

Choose an engine for your platform, programming language, and editing needs. Give the agent a fixed version, official APIs, and a working starting point.

Path step

Build the loop

Implement movement, interaction, scoring, and restart in small steps. Run the game and inspect screenshots after each change to build a playable loop.

Path step

Create the assets

Set the art direction, sprite dimensions, frame counts, and anchors before generating or finding assets. Check transparency, collision shapes, and animation states on import.

Path step

Playtest & iterate

Combine scripted inputs, state assertions, and key screenshots. Track build, gameplay, and visual issues separately, then playtest with people and adjust the pacing.

Path step

Ship your world

Build for the target platform and check asset paths, controls, and loading. Record dependency versions, generation prompts, and known limits for the next iteration.

Path step

Plan & scope

Define the camera, character controls, core interactions, and target hardware. Start with one room or level to keep the scope of the 3D project manageable.

Path step

Choose an engine

Choose the engine, renderer, and physics approach, then connect MCP or editor automation. Plan for both code changes and scene or asset operations in the editor.

Path step

Build the loop

Build movement, camera controls, collisions, and key interactions in a graybox level. Give the agent runtime state and errors as feedback while developing the gameplay.

Path step

Create the assets

After generating or finding models, check scale, topology, materials, rigs, and animation. Prepare assets that the engine can load and use reliably.

Path step

Playtest & iterate

Test scene connectivity, character behavior, physics stability, and frame times in the engine. Evaluate generated results with task checks and visual evidence.

Path step

Ship your world

Package for the target platform, trim unused assets, and verify loading. Record engine and plugin versions, hardware requirements, and reproduction steps.

Path step

Define the state

Decide whether code, an explicit scene, or video latents represent the world. Evaluate editability, interpretability, and visual quality separately.

Path step

Connect actions

Define the action space and environment interface. Distinguish language commands, keyboard inputs, and camera paths so model controls match the intended interaction.

Path step

Code the dynamics

Explore programs that express state transitions and rewards, or agents that update the environment. Check long-term state, object persistence, and editing capabilities.

Path step

Render the world

Pass structural conditions from the engine to a neural renderer. Check geometry, action alignment, temporal consistency, and inference latency separately.

Path step

Test consistency

Measure long-term drift, action response, object identity, and collisions. Distinguish project demonstrations, paper evaluations, and reproducible open implementations.

Path step

Build an experience

Choose a research demo or product prototype based on model licenses, compute costs, and real-time requirements. Keep reproducible configurations and documented limits.
